picks.title: 8 Stealth Taxes That Can Leave the IRS a Tip
picks.why: Taylor Schulte argues that your tax bracket understates what your next dollar of income really costs, because crossing certain income lines adds surtaxes, phases out deductions or raises Medicare premiums. He also makes the case that some of those lines are worth crossing on purpose. The useful takeaway is a simple three-scenario test to run before locking in year-end Roth conversions or gain harvesting. His audience is near Medicare age, so a few of the eight matter less for younger early retirees.

picks.show: Money For the Rest of Us
picks.search: Money For the Rest of Us
picks.title: Stock Pickers Keep Losing, Who's Winning?
picks.why: David Stein explains why active managers keep falling further behind even as their skill improves: index flows themselves push up the stocks that indexes already hold. He walks through research on who actually sells to index funds (mostly companies and insiders) and how much a dollar of passive flow moves prices, plus a San Francisco Fed paper on whether boomer retirement will drag on stocks. He closes with ways to own index funds without piling further into the S&P 500.

picks.title: Rob Arnott on the Hidden Costs of Passive Investing and the Real Winners From AI
picks.why: Rob Arnott argues that owning today's AI leaders is not the same as owning tomorrow's AI winners, and that cap-weighted index funds pay a real cost when stocks are added to the index, one that never shows up in the expense ratio. He makes the case for weighting by business size instead of market value. He also argues that GPU spending and depreciation are turning Big Tech into capital-heavy businesses, which matters for anyone whose index fund is now dominated by them.

picks.title: A Conversation With The Wealthy Barber
picks.why: Dave Chilton says most retirees get no advice at all on the order in which to draw down their accounts, and that tax-smart sequencing can be worth tens of thousands of dollars without adding any risk. He also pushes back on drawing tax-deferred accounts down early as a one-size-fits-all rule (Canada's "RRSP meltdown", a close cousin of the US Roth conversion ladder), and Ben Felix goes further, calling the blanket version irresponsible. It is Canada-specific in places, but the sequencing logic carries over.

picks.title: Dr. Daniel Crosby on Behaviorally Optimal Portfolios, Risk Composure and the Casino Myth
picks.why: Daniel Crosby argues that the best portfolio is the one you won't abandon, so he builds separate sleeves for safety, stability and growth instead of one optimized mix. He cites SEI research finding that clients holding a 6 to 24 month safety bucket were about ten times less likely to bail to cash in 2008, a behavioral case for cash buckets beyond the math. His stability sleeve is an unusual equal mix of large growth, small value, mid value, gold and intermediate Treasuries, and he splits risk into tolerance, capacity and "risk composure", meaning how likely panic is to override the other two.

picks.title: Q&A: I'm the Executor of Dad's $500K Portfolio. Should I Cash It Out?
picks.why: The bond question is the standout: a caller's long-term Treasury index fund fell 38% over six years, and the hosts argue that individual bonds take the same interest-rate loss even when no statement shows it. Joe Saul-Sehy calls short-term bonds a drag that barely keeps up with inflation and prefers T-bills for cash, while Paula Pant is buying 30-year Treasuries near 5.2% to 5.5% to hold to maturity. The hosts also disagree on whether an executor should move an inherited portfolio to cash during probate.

picks.title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods
picks.why: Lindsay Owens argues that pricing algorithms and AI shopping agents are ending the idea of a fixed price. In one test, 75% of 23 Instacart items were priced differently for different shoppers, with gaps of up to 23%, and AI agents told to find the cheapest option still steered users to pricier ones using their email and financial data. The episode doesn't discuss inflation statistics, but if prices become personal, the inflation a household actually lives through could drift from the CPI that inflation-linked bonds and withdrawal rules track.

picks.title: Episode 547: The RPR Reddit Forum, A Great Many Topics On Portfolios And Taxes, And Portfolio Reviews
picks.why: Frank Vasquez is the counterweight to the "Beyond Bonds" pitch below: he argues that covered call funds mostly change how payouts show up rather than total return, and that many new income ETFs are higher-fee packaging of old exposures. He also covers a listener rebuild of trend-following returns back to 1971 for backtesting managed futures, and the case for resetting withdrawal order and Roth conversions every year from tax brackets, health costs and income mix instead of following a fixed sequence. It leans on gold, so it's a good stress test if you don't.

picks.title: What If This Is the Worst Time to Retire?
picks.why: Ben Carlson and Christine Benz take on sequence-of-returns risk after a long bull market, and how today's higher yields change the withdrawal math. They cover buckets, front-loading spending, delaying Social Security and the case for a plain 60/40, and per the show notes they also weigh structured income products. It's a good check on whether an elaborate retirement income setup is doing more work than it needs to.

picks.title: AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin's Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?
picks.why: The first eight minutes are Ken Griffin saying AI is probably a bubble, and there's a long section on France's debt crisis. It's worth it for anyone uneasy about how much of a total-market fund now rides on AI, and for a bigger dose of sovereign debt stress than most FI shows give.

picks.title: #655 Vincent Deluard: The S&P Is Hiding a Bear Market
picks.why: Vincent Deluard, StoneX's director of global macro strategy and a longtime bull who has turned bearish, argues that a handful of megacaps are propping up the cap-weighted S&P 500 while most stocks are weak. He reads tax collections as a real-time gauge of the economy and argues Europe looks like Japan around 2012. The concentration argument is the part with lasting value; his closing trade ideas in the yen, the Korean won and UK stocks are tactical.

picks.title: Talk Your Book: Beyond Bonds in Retirement
picks.why: Calamos's Matt Kaufman makes the strongest pitch yet for replacing part of a retirement bond allocation with buffered, principal-protected, autocall and option-income ETFs, which he says now do what annuities and structured notes used to with clearer fees and ETF tax treatment. He cites roughly an 8.75% one-year cap on the S&P 500 with full principal protection. It's a sponsored segment, and a fully protected one-year product is essentially T-bills plus call options: nominal, with no inflation protection, and a cap that shrinks when rates fall. Pair it with Risk Parity Radio 547 for the rebuttal.

picks.title: What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now
picks.why: Barclays strategist Alexander Altmann argues the market is still in the denial stage of an AI boom, with stress showing first in cash-poor neocloud lenders and data center bonds, much as 2007 trouble started at the edges before reaching banks. He says the idea that AI spending is immune to higher interest rates is wrong, because heavy corporate bond issuance is now competing for limited capital even as rates stay high. He also expects most of next year's S&P 500 earnings growth to come from the AI ecosystem, which is a concrete way to see how much an index fund now rides on one theme.

picks.title: The S&P 500 Is Just 50 Stocks. The Nasdaq Is a 67% AI Bet. Kai Wu on What Else Is Hiding in Your Funds
picks.why: Sparkline Capital's Kai Wu looks through fund labels to show how the S&P 500, the Nasdaq, AI theme funds, emerging markets and even dividend and low-volatility funds can lean on the same companies and the same AI spending cycle. He argues that the number of holdings overstates diversification, and that cutting AI infrastructure exposure usually means loading up on the laggards instead, which is its own bet. Useful for anyone who owns several index funds and assumes they are spread out.

picks.title: J Scott Explains the Economic Domino Effect of an Energy Shock
picks.why: Investor and author J Scott walks through how an energy supply shock travels: oil futures move at once, gasoline follows within a week or two, and the effects work through supply chains into inflation and mortgage rates for months or years. He adds tariffs and deglobalization as extra pressure and asks whether the Federal Reserve can bring inflation down without stalling growth. A plain-language primer on the inflation channel that matters most to anyone living off a portfolio.

picks.title: Tech is Selling Off. AI Debt Fears Are Rising. So Why Does a $4B Manager See a Reverse Bubble?
picks.why: Money manager Jay Hatfield makes the bull case against the AI bubble story: much of the buildout runs on long-term compute contracts with investment-grade tenants, priced below today's spot rates, which makes it look more like contracted infrastructure than speculation. He pairs that with a rule of thumb linking the 10-year Treasury yield to the expected peak Fed funds rate and stock valuations, and explains why he avoids long Treasuries near 5%. Worth hearing for anyone uneasy about how much of a total market fund now rides on AI, because it is the strongest version of the other side.

picks.title: Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Greatest Business Ever? Google's $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions
picks.why: The hosts dig into Anthropic's IPO filing and its margins, and argue over whether Alphabet's post-earnings drop overshot. The part most relevant to long-horizon investors is the debate about AI borrowing: how much debt the buildout could add to bond markets, what that might do to Treasury yields, and how concentrated the economy has become in a handful of companies. The closing segment on the midterms can be skipped.

picks.title: 781. Ten Things I Do to Spend Peacefully
picks.why: Doc G, a retired physician, lays out ten habits that let him spend in retirement without second-guessing every purchase, set against ideas like Die With Zero. It treats the spending phase as a problem of anxiety and decision fatigue rather than of withdrawal-rate math, which is the part many careful savers find hardest after years of accumulating.

picks.title: Episode 548: The Intersection of Biased Skepticism, Shark Jumping (From Ep. 532), And Personal Finance Hoarding Culture
picks.why: Frank Vasquez responds to recent Early Retirement Now critiques of risk parity style portfolios, arguing that ERN's own toolbox gave a mix of US stocks, small cap value, Treasuries and gold a noticeably higher safe withdrawal rate than a classic 75/25 stock and bond mix, with the biggest gap at the worst historical starting points. He also argues that planning very long retirements to end with a large leftover balance amounts to hoarding, and that gold backtests using pre-1971 data mislead because gold was pegged to the dollar. It is one side of a public debate, but a sharp challenge to conservative withdrawal assumptions; the toolbox results come about 11 minutes in and the hoarding discussion near the end.

picks.title: Chip Stocks Look Cheap. AI Spending Is Surging. So Why Is Cameron Dawson Watching for Peak Earnings?
picks.why: NewEdge Wealth CIO Cameron Dawson looks at the AI chip trade from the earnings side rather than the valuation side. Her concern is that semiconductor profits could be near a cyclical peak, in which case today's modest price-to-earnings ratios are the classic trap of cyclical stocks looking cheapest at the top. A useful counterpoint to the more bullish AI cases going around, and a reminder to ask how durable the earnings behind a low multiple really are.

picks.search: The Psychology of Money Morgan Housel
picks.title: The Hardest Financial Skill
picks.why: Morgan Housel reads a short essay built on one of his best-known ideas, that the hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving, then takes listener questions on returns from AI, how to think about bubbles, and making your younger self proud. A short, reflective listen on knowing when you have enough, which matters as much in the spending years as in the saving ones.

picks.title: Vanguard
picks.why: Ben Gilbert and David Rosenthal tell the full story of Vanguard, from John Bogle's firing at Wellington in 1974 and the unusual mutual ownership structure he built in response, through the rise of index funds, the ETF debate, 2008, Buffett's bet against hedge funds and the firm's first outside CEO. At close to four hours it is a long listen, but it is the best single account of how low-cost indexing went from a fringe idea to the default for millions of investors, and why Vanguard's structure lets it keep cutting fees.

picks.title: The $300 Billion Structured Notes Market Is Booming
picks.why: Nomura's Alex Micalizzi explains how structured notes pair a bank IOU with a derivative, why US sales are on pace for roughly $300 billion this year, and how they have become a popular way for individual investors to bet on AI. A clear look at how these products are built and priced, and at a large pool of AI exposure that sits outside the usual index funds and ETFs.

picks.title: Talk Your Book: Diversifying the AI Trade
picks.why: Nuveen's Brian Griggs talks through ways to own the AI buildout without piling further into mega-cap tech, from municipal bonds with high tax-equivalent yields to private money moving from data centers toward real assets and farmland, plus when to rebalance. It is a sponsored Talk Your Book episode, so treat it as a pitch, but it is a useful map of what diversifying away from the AI trade can look like.

picks.title: Seven Stocks Are 41% of the S&P | John Davi on Building Portfolios Beyond the Mag 7 Bet
picks.why: Astoria's John Davi, who builds ETF model portfolios, explains how he trimmed an equity overweight without calling a top and why he would move the classic 60/40 toward roughly 50% stocks, 30% bonds and 20% diversifiers such as real assets. He also suggests watching credit default swaps on the companies funding the AI buildout as an early warning sign, favoring AI adopters over AI builders, and using a quality screen to stay in growth stocks without riding the seven largest names. A practical take on what to do about index concentration rather than just worrying about it.

picks.title: The Liquidity Cycle Has Turned | Michael Howell on What It Means for Investors
picks.why: Michael Howell of CrossBorder Capital argues that the global liquidity cycle has turned, and that slowing liquidity can weigh on stocks even while AI earnings stay strong, because real-economy investment and a wall of maturing debt now compete with markets for the same funding. He measures liquidity as the financial system's capacity to fund rather than by the policy rate, walks through the four phases of his cycle and the role of bank reserves, repo, collateral and Treasury issuance, and makes a case for government bonds as liquidity tightens. He also touches on China's debt and what it could mean for gold. A useful macro lens that most retirement-focused shows never cover.

picks.title: Breaking Down Our Investment Portfolios
picks.why: Ben Felix and Dan Bortolotti open up their own portfolios and explain how they got there: Dan holds a simple 70/30 ETF mix, while Ben runs 100% equities with global diversification and factor tilts. They trace their views back to early influences, the 2008 crisis and research on wealth and happiness, and cover homeownership and cash reserves along the way. It opens with a physician describing how the show changed his approach to financial planning. A rare look at how two evidence-based advisors actually invest their own money, and why they ended up in different places.

picks.title: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami
picks.why: Skanda Amarnath of Employ America joins Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway to work through what this week's Democratic midterm gains could mean for the economy and markets: the future makeup of the Fed's rate-setting committee, the fight against inflation, tariffs, and the AI data center buildout. A fast, well-informed first read on the election's macro consequences while they are still fresh.

picks.title: Stocks Are Falling. The Economy Is Weakening. So Why Doesn't Mike Green See Passive Flows Turning?
picks.why: Mike Green of Tier1 Alpha makes his case that passive investing now shapes stock prices: steady retirement contributions flow through target date funds and market cap weighted indexes into the largest companies, while liquidity in those stocks doesn't grow with their market value. He explains how those flows may drive concentration and factor behavior, where valuation analysis still fits, and what could interrupt the buying, with employment trends the thing to watch. Useful for anyone who owns index funds and wants the strongest version of the critique of what passive flows do to the market.

picks.title: SocGen's Albert Edwards on 10% Yields and a 50% to 60% Drop | #656
picks.why: Societe Generale's long-standing bear Albert Edwards lays out why he thinks fiscal dominance could push central banks toward money printing, send the 10-year Treasury yield toward 10% and take the S&P 500 down 50% to 60%, with stocks and bonds falling together. He also covers China's weakening credit impulse, oil and food prices, what the IPO boom says about the cycle, and gold as a debasement hedge. An extreme view, but a clear one, and worth hearing as a stress test for any portfolio that counts on bonds to cushion a stock decline.

picks.title: Tech is Selling Off. Spending Is Outrunning Wages. What Happens When the Wealth Effect Fades?
picks.why: Bob Elliott of Unlimited and Aahan Menon of Prometheus Research argue that stock market gains are letting households spend faster than wages grow, and ask what happens to corporate profits if that wealth effect fades. They debate whether bonds look better than stocks or cash, how persistent inflation ties the Fed's hands, and whether AI is delivering the productivity and revenue gains outside tech needed to justify its investment boom. Both separate these risks from a 2008-style credit crisis, which makes it a measured counterpoint to the more dramatic bear cases.

picks.title: First Friday: Stocks Crashed. Jobs Boomed. Now What?
picks.why: The monthly economic roundup takes on a strange week: a record one-day loss in tech stocks, with the S&P 500 down 4.4% and the Nasdaq in correction, set against a jobs report that came in near three times expectations. It covers what concentration risk means for index fund investors when a sell-off starts in AI stocks, inflation running ahead of wage growth, a Fed hold with two members dissenting in favor of a hike, and a rule of thumb for where the 10-year Treasury tends to trade and what today's yield implies about inflation expectations. It also notes the 3.6% Social Security raise and the higher Medicare premiums that eat into it. One of the first calm walk-throughs of the sell-off.

picks.title: Jim Dahle: Is Avoiding Taxes Costing You Money?
picks.why: White Coat Investor founder Jim Dahle, who calls himself a recovering optimizer, talks with Morningstar's hosts about when cash, nominal bonds and TIPS each earn a place in a portfolio, how he thinks about direct indexing and tax-loss harvesting, and which strategies belong on the too-hard pile. The thread running through it is the case that chasing the last bit of tax savings can cost more than it saves. A useful check for anyone whose tax-efficiency rules have started to complicate their portfolio.

picks.title: Blue Wave Sell-Off. Four Market Pros on What Comes Next
picks.why: The show's monthly Last Call recap brings four quick interviews recorded after the post-election sell-off. Brent Kochuba of SpotGamma explains how options dealer positioning can amplify selling into November expiration; Ben Hunt argues the midterms clarified the limits of presidential power and handed governors more say over data center permits; Aahan Menon ties falling AI stocks to consumer spending through the wealth effect; and Eric Pachman tracks diesel and freight costs through producer prices to show how many industries face unusual cost increases, along with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's emergency oil loans. Four different lenses on the same week, each in a few minutes.

picks.title: Episode 551: Stop Chasing Yield, The Limitations Of International Diversification, And Portfolio Reviews As Of November 6, 2026
picks.why: Frank Vasquez argues that autocallable, high-income and covered call funds mostly change how a payout is delivered rather than improving returns, and that forced income means forced taxes in a taxable account, so selling shares beats buying a built-in retirement paycheck. He then challenges global stock funds as largely a currency bet rather than real business diversification, suggests managed futures as a more deliberate currency tool, and makes the case that splitting value from growth protects better in a drawdown than splitting US from international. A sharp counterpoint to two very common portfolio habits.
